children: The Nifty may still be significantly higher than where it was five years ago in rupee terms, but for a dollar-based investor, much of that gain has been erased by the depreciation of the Indian currency.
What the chart is really showing

The chart shows the Nifty measured in US dollars has fallen back to around 242, a level last seen around September 2021. In other words, despite the sharp rise in the headline Nifty over the past five years, the return looks far less impressive once the rupee's decline against the dollar is considered.
The key takeaway from the chart is not that the Nifty has gone nowhere in five years. In rupee terms, the index has risen substantially.
The issue is what happens when that return is converted back into dollars.

The Nifty has moved from roughly the 17,500 area in September 2021 to around 23,200 currently. But the rupee has weakened from around the mid-70s against the dollar to close to Rs 96. That currency depreciation has absorbed a large part of the equity-market gains for a dollar-based investor.
This also explains why the recent currency weakness matters beyond the forex market. When the rupee falls sharply, India's headline equity performance can look considerably weaker in dollar terms.

The timing is significant. The rupee has recently come under renewed pressure, closing at around 96 per dollar on September 16, its weakest level in more than a month. Brent crude was above $108 a barrel, while rising US Treasury yields and expectations of tighter US monetary policy added to pressure on the currency.
Foreign flows, oil prices add another pressure point
Foreign investors have also turned sellers again. FPIs withdrew about Rs 14,116 crore from Indian equities in the first half of September, after remaining net buyers for the last 2 months.
The outflows come amid surge in Brent crude prices. So far this month, oil prices have risen over 20 percent, creating a key headwind for markets.

Higher oil prices are particularly important for India because the country is a major crude importer. A weaker rupee makes those imports even more expensive in domestic currency, creating another pressure point for inflation and corporate margins.
The combination has already been visible in the equity market. The Nifty has already fallen 4 percent in the past one month, while the broader market also remains under pressure.

title: Nifty in dollar terms back to September 2021 levels as rupee, oil weigh on returns
